# Compact full-shape intrinsic lifts over the original lattice

This is a compactification and depth-transfer theorem for a FIXED finite
integer projection. It does not prove OC. Unlike a weak density lift, it
retains every residual convex fiber before passing to a limit. Unlike an
integer graph lift, it retains the original integer rank. The cost is a
larger continuous ambient dimension and lower-dimensional integer fibers.
No fine lattice is transported through the auxiliary continuous maps.

## 1. Statement and notation

Let k>=0 and m>=1. Let P be a finite nonempty lattice-convex subset of
Z^k that affinely spans R^k; lattice-convex means

    P=conv(P) intersect Z^k.

For each l let K_(l,z), z in P, be m-dimensional convex bodies in R^m.
Assume they are compatible: for every anchored convex representation
z=sum_a lambda_a z_a, with z,z_a in P and nonnegative coefficients of
sum one,

    sum_a lambda_a K_(l,z_a) subset K_(l,z).               (1)

Let M_l=sum_z |K_(l,z)|. Assume

    |K_(l,z)|/M_l -> p_z>0  for every z in P.              (2)

The components P_1,...,P_s are generated by joining the target and all
positive-coefficient sources in every nontrivial anchored representation.
Let L(P) be the vector space of scalar functions on P preserving all
these representations. Put ell=dim L(P) and

    t=ell-k-1,       D=sm+t.

There exist full-dimensional convex bodies B_l in R^k times R^D with
exactly the integer fibers P, each fiber of affine dimension m, and a
subsequence with the following properties.

* The normalized intrinsic H_m mass of each z-fiber is |K_(l,z)|/M_l;
  total H_m mass is exactly one.
* All lifted fibers lie in fixed affine m-planes and a common bounded
  set. Each converges in Hausdorff distance to a positive-volume convex
  body in its own plane. Their hull B_* is again full dimensional with
  exactly these fibers.
* A global affine map F_l, fixing the integer base, sends the lifted
  mixed set onto the original mixed set and pushes its intrinsic H_m
  measure to the original mixed measure divided by M_l.
* Writing D_max for maximum normalized closed-halfspace depth, one has

    D_max(original_l) >= D_max(lift_l),
    D_max(lift_l) -> D_max(lift_*).                       (3)

Every containing ambient halfspace, including one carrying boundary
mass, is included in these statements. Moreover

    s<=2^k,   ell<=2^k,
    m<=D<=(m+1)2^k-k-1.                                 (4)

For k=0, P is a singleton, s=ell=1, t=0, and D=m.

## 2. Elementary facts about the components and L(P)

Every anchored representation uses only one component, by definition.
Thus each component indicator belongs to L(P), and restrictions to the
components split L(P) as their direct sum. A component is P-closed:
if z in P belongs to conv(P_i), a representation either is trivial or
joins z to its sources in P_i. Hence z belongs to P_i.

There is a finite matrix A with kernel L(P) whose rows have the form

    e_z-sum_a lambda_a e_(z_a).                           (5)

Indeed the space spanned by all such rows is finite dimensional, so a
finite selection spans it. Each component is generated by finitely many
such representations as well. Fix these selections once and for all.

Since P affinely spans R^k, the functions 1,z_1,...,z_k are independent
members of L(P). Complete them to a basis by G_1,...,G_t. Set
G(z)=(G_1(z),...,G_t(z)). The graph (z,G(z)) affinely spans R^(k+t).
Otherwise a nonzero affine relation among its coordinates would
contradict basis independence.

For completeness, ell<=h(P)<=2^k. The second inequality is Doignon's
theorem applied to convex sets together with conv(P). For the first,
the graph (z,G(z)) preserves all anchored representations in both
directions: projection recovers the reverse direction. It therefore
preserves all convexly closed traces and the finite Helly number.
Any finite set of affine dimension ell-1 has Helly number at least ell:
take the ell facets of a simplex with ell affinely independent vertices
in that set. Their total intersection is empty and the intersection of
any ell-1 contains the omitted vertex. This also covers ell=1 by the
one-member empty-set example.

Finally different components cannot contain points of the same parity.
Their integer midpoint belongs to P and its representation joins them.
Selecting one point in each component therefore gives s<=2^k. These
facts prove (4), apart from the already evident D>=m.

## 3. Shape normalization with a common volume factor

For large l, all normalized volumes in (2) lie in [eta,1] for a fixed
eta>0. For each component i choose an anchor. There is an invertible
linear map T_(l,i) with

    |det T_(l,i)|=1/M_l                                 (6)

such that the transformed anchor has uniformly bounded diameter.

Here are the volume details. The maximum-inscribed-simplex normalization
has linear part A and gives an anchor translate Q with
B_2^m subset Q subset R B_2^m, R=m(m+2). Consequently

    kappa_m <= |det A| |K_anchor| <= kappa_m R^m.

The scalar multiple T=(M_l |det A|)^(-1/m) A satisfies (6), and the
scalar factor is bounded above and below by constants depending only
on m and eta. Translations are irrelevant to diameter.

Use this SAME T_(l,i) for every fiber in P_i. Their volumes now lie in
[eta,1]. Their diameters are uniformly bounded. One way to see this
with no eccentricity assumption is the quantitative two-body lemma in
`candidate c0cb4d49afb99df3`:
if a source K occurs with coefficient lambda>0 in a target L, then
lambda K+u subset L, so

    K+L subset (1+lambda^(-1))L-lambda^(-1)u.

Together with eta<=|K|,|L|<=1 this bounds |K+L|/|K| and
|L|/|K| in the sense needed for two-sided difference-body comparison.
The lemma's constants depend only on m,eta,lambda. Its proof is a
maximal-simplex normalization, a ball-plus-segment volume estimate,
and a simplex inner-ball estimate; it has no OC dependency. Along the
fixed finite incidence chains, diameter control propagates from the
anchor to every fiber. Equivalently one may use Section 3 of
`candidate dbf3b23d25004153`.

Write Q_(l,z)=T_(l,i)K_(l,z) for z in P_i, and let c_(l,z) be its
centroid. Since each anchored representation lies in one component,
the Q family still satisfies (1). Both c_(l,z) and the corresponding
convex combination of source centroids lie in Q_(l,z), so every row
(5), applied to c_l, has norm at most the common diameter bound.

Orthogonally project c_l onto L(P) tensor R^m, obtaining g_l. The
nonzero singular values of the fixed finite matrix A give a uniform
bound on ||c_l-g_l||. If A=0 the difference is zero. Define

    R_(l,z)=Q_(l,z)-g_(l,z).                             (7)

All these residual bodies lie in a common ball. They satisfy every
anchored compatibility inclusion because g_l preserves each such
representation. Their volumes are |K_(l,z)|/M_l.

## 4. Orthogonal block and continuous graph construction

Decompose R^D as (R^m)^s times R^t and let E_i:R^m -> (R^m)^s be
the isometric inclusion in block i, with zero in every other block.
For z in P_i define the lifted fiber

    L_(l,z)={(E_i x,G(z)): x in R_(l,z)}.                 (8)

Set B_l=conv union_z ({z} times L_(l,z)). These lifts satisfy every
anchored inclusion: all nonzero sources belong to the target component,
E_i is linear, G preserves the representation, and the residual bodies
are compatible. Therefore the z-fiber of B_l is exactly L_(l,z).
Its integer projection is exactly P, since P is lattice-convex.

Each fiber lies in a FIXED affine m-plane and its parametrization (8)
is an isometry. Thus H_m(L_(l,z))=|R_(l,z)|. Distinct integer fibers
are disjoint; their finite sum is the H_m measure of their union, whose
Hausdorff dimension is m and whose total measure is one.

The hull is full dimensional, not merely a relative body. Its affine
direction space contains each of the s complete m-blocks, because at
least one positive m-volume fiber occurs in each block. Modulo these
block directions, its projected graph (z,G(z)) has affine dimension
k+t by Section 2. Therefore its affine dimension is sm+k+t=k+D.

To recover the original body, put h_(l,z)=T_(l,i)^(-1)g_(l,z) on P_i.
Because each anchored relation stays within one component, h_l belongs
to L(P) tensor R^m. There are b_l, a matrix A_l on the integer-base
coordinates, and a matrix U_l on R^t such that

    h_(l,z)=b_l+A_l z+U_l G(z).

Define the global affine map

    F_l(z,X_1,...,X_s,tau)
       =(z, sum_i T_(l,i)^(-1)X_i+b_l+A_l z+U_l tau).    (9)

On (8), the second coordinate is T_(l,i)^(-1)(x+g_(l,z)),
which ranges exactly over K_(l,z). The m-dimensional Jacobian on
each fiber is |det T_(l,i)^(-1)|=M_l, COMMON to every component.
Hence the pushforward of lifted intrinsic measure is precisely the
original mixed measure divided by M_l.

For any original halfspace containing F_l(y), its inverse image under
F_l is a closed affine halfspace containing y, or the whole lifted
ambient space. It cannot be empty. The whole-space case contributes
mass one; all depths are at most one. Taking infima proves the first
inequality in (3), pointwise for every y before taking maxima.

## 5. Exact component isolation and continuity of depth

The component indicators belong to L(P), so each is the restriction
of an affine function I_i(z,tau) on the graph coordinates. It is one
on P_i and zero on every other component.

Fix a center in component i. Any affine halfspace cut on that component
extends to a halfspace of the full lifted ambient space. Subtracting
T(1-I_i) from its affine defining function leaves its values on
component i unchanged and makes it strictly negative on every other
component when T is sufficiently large. Such a finite T exists because
all the other component sets are compact. This works for closed cuts:
other components are strictly excluded, while any boundary mass in
component i is retained. If the desired restricted cut is the entire
component, I_i-1/2 isolates it directly.

Consequently, if a_(l,i)=sum_(z in P_i)|R_(l,z)| and depth_i uses the
normalized measure of the lifted component alone, then pointwise

    depth_lift(y)=a_(l,i) depth_i(y),    y in component i. (10)

Restriction gives the lower bound in (10); the preceding extension
gives the upper bound. Therefore

    D_max(lift_l)=max_i a_(l,i) D_max(component_(l,i)).    (11)

Within one component all fibers have the SAME m-block direction. If
the center moves by v in that block, a halfspace with nonzero block
coefficient can be translated so its boundary continues to contain the
center; normalize that coefficient to length one. Every component
fiber's threshold moves by at most |v|, independently of the base and
graph coefficients. Fibers in a ball of radius R have intervening slab
volume at most kappa_(m-1) R^(m-1)|v|. Halfspaces with zero block
coefficient are unchanged by this movement. Taking infima yields a
uniform Lipschitz bound for depth_i, since a_(l,i) is bounded below.

Take a subsequence for which every residual body converges in Hausdorff
distance. All limiting volumes are p_z>0 by (2). Compatibility passes
to the limit by approximating source points with fixed coefficients.
Convex-body indicators converge in L1 in each fixed m-plane: off the
null boundary of a full-dimensional convex limit, interior and exterior
membership eventually stabilize. Thus each component's normalized
measures converge in total variation. This gives uniform convergence
of depths at fixed centers, and the preceding Lipschitz estimate
handles moving centers.

Each component has compact candidate fibers and a continuous depth
function on them, so its maximum exists. A subsequence of maximizers
with fixed base gives the upper limit inequality; approximating a
limit maximizer in that same fiber gives the lower limit inequality.
Hence its maximum depth converges. Formula (11) proves the second
claim of (3). The limiting hull is full dimensional and has exactly
the limiting fibers by the argument in Section 4.

## 6. Zero limiting weights and the precise limitation

If initially some normalized masses tend to zero, retain
P_+={z:p_z>0}. Compatibility with any one positive source shows P_+ is
lattice-convex: a target containing lambda K_z plus a translation has
normalized mass at least lambda^m p_z. Its total relative mass tends
to one. Restricting to its fibers can only decrease a center's
unnormalized cap mass, so

    D_max(original_l)
       >= (M_(l,+)/M_l) D_max(restricted_l).              (12)

The retained family is exactly realized by its convex hull. If P_+
has smaller affine rank, first identify its affine integer lattice
with Z^(k') using a saturated lattice basis. This changes only the
integer coordinates; every m-fiber Jacobian is one. Apply the theorem
at rank k'. Nothing here permits dropping positive intrinsic mass.

The theorem yields a compact dominating lift and an exact prelimit
depth comparison for coarse uniform fiber measures. It does NOT say
that a fine lattice inside the m continuous coordinates remains dense
after the maps T_(l,i); these maps can mix and rescale its directions.
It also does not give the original sharp constant merely by applying
a dimension-based theorem to the lift: its continuous ambient
dimension is D, whose Gamma_D can be smaller than Gamma_m. The depth
comparison and the dimension bound are proved; a global sharp mass
allocation or fine-lattice recovery is not supplied.
